summary.summary: Kirklees' debt keeps climbing: external borrowing rose £42.8m to £816.8m in 2025/26 (against a £987.2m capital financing requirement), funded by £90m of new PWLB loans at 4.59%-4.72% and £32.5m of medium-term loans from other councils, while treasury investments halved to £30.2m. £96.5m of loans fall due within 12 months against that £30.2m of cash, and the council says it will keep borrowing short-to-medium term while long rates stay high. The year had genuine positives: a £5.5m treasury budget underspend and a restructuring that prepaid £40m of Barclays loans for £29.5m — a £10.5m discount worth £2.1m in NPV savings. It still holds £30.8m of LOBO loans (none called in-year) and a £10m CCLA property fund position carrying £1.3m of unrealised losses behind the statutory override, now expected to run to April 2029.

signals.headline: External borrowing up £42.8m to £816.8m at 31 March 2026; £90m new PWLB plus £32.5m of local-authority loans taken in-year
signals.why: The CFR is still rising with the capital programme (£987.2m), so Kirklees is a committed repeat borrower.

signals.headline: £96.5m of loans mature within 12 months of 31 March 2026 (up from £75.2m a year earlier), by a deliberate short/medium-term borrowing strategy while long rates are high
signals.why: A growing short-dated stack must be rolled at whatever rates prevail after the sharp market moves of March 2026.

signals.headline: Treasury investments halved to £30.2m at 31 March 2026 (from £58.6m), against £816.8m of debt and £96.5m maturing within a year
signals.why: Year-end cash covers less than a third of the debt due in the next 12 months, leaving little buffer for shocks.

news_drafts.headline: Kirklees schools' high needs deficit stands at £82.2m, with the annual shortfall down £3m to £17m
news_drafts.lead:
Kirklees Council's accumulated overspend on support for children with special educational needs and disabilities (the "high needs" part of school funding) stood at £82.2m at 31 March 2026, according to papers for the Cabinet meeting on 6 October. The shortfall built up in the year to March 2026 was £17m, £3m lower than the £20m of the year before.

The council's medium-term financial strategy (its financial plan for the next few years) says "progress is being made in Kirklees". The deficit is on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools. It is held under the statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet.

The government's Safety Valve Programme, an agreement under which the council had been working on this deficit, ended in February 2026. The council now receives 90% of its historic deficits' cost through the High Needs Stability Grant and must meet the remaining 10% from its general fund, the main account that pays for day-to-day services. The papers estimate that at about £13m across 2026/27 and 2027/28. Separately, the cost of the treasury management (borrowing and cash handling) needed to carry the deficit is about £3.4m a year.

findings.headline: Freehold reversion property sales will result in £38,389 annual rental income loss
findings.detail: The council owns freehold interests on many disposal assets and currently receives rental income from them. Disposing of these freehold reversions to the existing tenants will generate capital receipts but at the cost of lost annual rental income.
findings.matters: Shows the revenue-capital trade-off councils make when pursuing capital receipts; £38k annual cost is material for ongoing budget planning.
findings.quote: Freehold reversions do result in the loss of annual income to the Council in the case of the assets in Appendix A this amounts to £38,389.08.

findings.headline: Sale of Scarr End Lane will eliminate requirement for substantial ongoing remedial works on unstable land
findings.detail: The 5.34-acre site has experienced multiple land failures since 2023 due to steep embankment instability. A structural survey confirms ongoing physical weathering and significant remedial measures are required to stabilise the land. Disposal transfers this liability to the new owner and removes the council's requirement to undertake an extended remediation programme.
findings.matters: Converting a known future liability into a present capital receipt improves the council's financial position and removes exposure to ongoing remediation costs.
findings.quote: Disposal of the site would transfer these responsibilities and remove the requirement for the Council to undertake a substantial programme of remedial works over an extended period.

findings.headline: Council identifying additional surplus assets to cover disposals pipeline shortfalls
findings.detail: The council recognizes that some assets may fail to sell or achieve lower values. It is proactively identifying additional contingency assets beyond immediate targets to feed the pipeline for future years and maintain the ability to hit annual capital receipt targets if some disposals stall.
findings.matters: Demonstrates whether a council has robust plans to deliver capital receipt targets and how it manages the risk that assets do not sell as anticipated.
findings.quote: further surplus assets need to be identified to feed the pipeline for future years and to cover any shortfall should assets fail to sell / be removed from the disposal process.

findings.headline: Council targets £4m annual capital receipts over four years to reduce borrowing needs
findings.detail: The council has set £4m capital receipts targets for each of 2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29 and 2029/30. It delivered £7.5m through disposals in 2025/26. The report explicitly identifies capital receipts as a strategy to reduce the need for borrowing to fund the capital plan.
findings.matters: Capital receipts strategy is how councils fund investment and manage debt levels. For a lender, this shows the council is actively managing its borrowing; for a peer finance director, it indicates a substantial multi-year programme.
findings.quote: Funds received from the sale of Council assets helps to reduce the need for borrowing.

findings.headline: Adults and Children's services receiving substantial additional investment (£15m and £12.2m respectively in 2027/28) to address demand and inflation; savings delivery risk noted.
findings.detail: Adults Services receives c£15m additional funding in 2027/28 (£4m demand-led, £11m care costs and CPI inflation), following a prior-quarter overspend of £10.7m. Children's Services receives £12.2m (£8.8m demand-led sufficiency, £3.1m inflation, £0.3m staffing). Over five years, Adults receive £99.2m and Children receive £26.2m additional funding. The paper notes past delays in delivering some savings proposals, particularly on Client Financial Affairs income and market reform savings.
findings.matters: Significant ongoing investment in social care reflects structural demand pressures; documented difficulties delivering savings on these budgets indicate material risk of future overspend.
findings.figures: Adults 2027/28: £15m additional; five-year total £99.2m; Children 2027/28: £12.2m; five-year total £26.2m; Adults Q1 2026/27 overspend £10.7m
findings.quote: There are currently significant in year budgetary pressures in Adult Services, mainly being driven by complexity of need and price increases in relation to placements. There are also savings targets are in place and in some cases, delays have been seen in the delivery of these
